In [[cryptography]], '''XTEA''' ('''eXtended TEA''') is a [[block cipher]] designed to correct weaknesses in [[Tiny Encryption Algorithm|TEA]]. The [[cipher]]'s designers were [[David Wheeler (computer scientist)|David Wheeler]] and [[Roger Needham]] of the [[University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory|Cambridge Computer Laboratory]], and the algorithm was presented in an unpublished technical report in 1997 (Needham and Wheeler, 1997). It is not subject to any [[patent]]s.<ref name=wheeler>{{Cite tech report |author1=Roger M. Needham |author2=David J. Wheeler |date=October 1997 |title=Tea extensions |url=http://www.cix.co.uk/~klockstone/xtea.pdf |work=Computer Laboratory, University of Cambridge}}</ref>

Like TEA, XTEA is a [[block size (cryptography)|64-bit block]] [[Feistel cipher]] with a [[cryptographic key length|128-bit key]] and a suggested 64 rounds. Several differences from TEA are apparent, including a somewhat more complex [[key schedule|key-schedule]] and a rearrangement of the shifts, [[XOR]]s, and additions.

==Implementations==
This standard [[C (programming language)|C]] source code, adapted from the reference code released into the [[public domain]] by David Wheeler and Roger Needham, encrypts and decrypts using XTEA:
<syntaxhighlight lang="C">
#include <stdint.h>

/* take 64 bits of data in v[0] and v[1] and 128 bits of key[0] - key[3] */

void encipher(unsigned int num_rounds, uint32_t v[2], uint32_t const key[4]) {
    unsigned int i;
    uint32_t v0=v[0], v1=v[1], sum=0, delta=0x9E3779B9;
    for (i=0; i < num_rounds; i++) {
        v0 += (((v1 << 4) ^ (v1 >> 5)) + v1) ^ (sum + key[sum & 3]);
        sum += delta;
        v1 += (((v0 << 4) ^ (v0 >> 5)) + v0) ^ (sum + key[(sum>>11) & 3]);
    }
    v[0]=v0; v[1]=v1;
}

void decipher(unsigned int num_rounds, uint32_t v[2], uint32_t const key[4]) {
    unsigned int i;
    uint32_t v0=v[0], v1=v[1], delta=0x9E3779B9, sum=delta*num_rounds;
    for (i=0; i < num_rounds; i++) {
        v1 -= (((v0 << 4) ^ (v0 >> 5)) + v0) ^ (sum + key[(sum>>11) & 3]);
        sum -= delta;
        v0 -= (((v1 << 4) ^ (v1 >> 5)) + v1) ^ (sum + key[sum & 3]);
    }
    v[0]=v0; v[1]=v1;
}
</syntaxhighlight>
The changes from the reference source code are minor:
* The reference source code used the <code>unsigned long</code> type rather than the [[64-bit]] clean <code>uint32_t</code>.
* The reference source code did not use <code>const</code> types.
* The reference source code omitted redundant parentheses, using C precedence to write the round function as e.g. <code>v1 += (v0<<4 ^ v0>>5) + v0 ^ sum + k[sum>>11 & 3]</code>;

The recommended value for the "num_rounds" parameter is 32, not 64, as each iteration of the loop does two Feistel-cipher rounds. To additionally improve speed, the loop can be unrolled by pre-computing the values of sum+key[].

==Cryptanalysis==
{{see also|Cryptanalysis}}
In 2004, Ko et al. presented a [[related-key attack|related-key]] [[differential attack]] on 27 out of 64 rounds of XTEA, requiring 2<sup>20.5</sup> [[chosen plaintext]]s and a [[time complexity]] of 2<sup>115.15</sup>.<ref>{{Cite conference |conference=FSE 2004 |last1=Ko |first1=Youngdai |last2=Hong |first2=Seokhie |last3=Lee |first3=Wonil |last4=Lee |first4=Sangjin |last5=Kang |first5=Ju-Sung |title=Related Key Differential Attacks on 27 Rounds of XTEA and Full-Round GOST |editor1=Roy, B. |editor2=Meier, W. |book-title=Fast Software Encryption |volume=3017 |date=2004 |pages=299–316 |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-25937-4_19 |doi-access=free |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |url=https://www.iacr.org/archive/fse2004/30170298/30170298.pdf |access-date=2018-10-10 |isbn=978-3-540-22171-5}}</ref><ref>{{Cite conference |last1=Hong |first1=Seokhie |last2=Hong |first2=Deukjo |last3=Ko |first3=Youngdai |last4=Chang |first4=Donghoon |last5=Lee |first5=Wonil |last6=Lee |first6=Sangjin |title=Differential Cryptanalysis of TEA and XTEA |editor1=Lim, JI. |editor2=Lee, DH. |book-title=Information Security and Cryptology |conference=ICISC 2003 |volume=2971 |date=2004 |pages=402–417 |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-24691-6_30 |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-540-21376-5}}</ref>

In 2009, Lu presented a related-key rectangle attack on 36 rounds of XTEA, breaking more rounds than any previously published cryptanalytic results for XTEA. The paper presents two attacks, one without and with a weak key assumption, which corresponds to 2<sup>64.98</sup> bytes of data and 2<sup>126.44</sup> operations, and 2<sup>63.83</sup> bytes of data and 2<sup>104.33</sup> operations respectively.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lu |first1=Jiqiang |title=Related-key rectangle attack on 36 rounds of the XTEA block cipher |journal=International Journal of Information Security |date=2 July 2008 |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=1–11 |doi=10.1007/s10207-008-0059-9 |language=en |s2cid=26794956 |issn=1615-5262}}</ref>

==Block TEA==
Presented along with XTEA was a variable-width block cipher termed '''Block TEA''', which uses the XTEA round function, but Block TEA applies it cyclically across an entire message for several iterations. Because it operates on the entire message, Block TEA has the property that it does not need a [[block cipher modes of operation|mode of operation]]. An attack on the full Block TEA was described by Saarinen,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Saarinen |first1=Markku-Juhani |title=Cryptanalysis of Block Tea |date=1998-10-20 |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/228548968 |access-date=2018-10-10 |website=ResearchGate}}</ref> which also details a weakness in Block TEA's successor, [[XXTEA]].
